critique.title: A record is not a reason to read
critique.text: The previous view proved that sources had been located, but did not show what the proposed page would teach. The replacement starts with a reader’s question, a substantive introduction and a sequence of explained sections.

critique.title: An excerpt is not an explanation
critique.text: Short windows left arguments unfinished and sometimes mixed commentary with notes. The replacement explains what each writer contributes, links the reading passage and labels material that still cannot support the proposed conclusion.

critique.title: Twenty-one records are not twenty-one separate pages
critique.text: The earlier list flattened whole guides, supporting comparisons and small reader aids into the same category. The replacement gives each proposal a role. Unity belongs inside Ephesians 4; the records stay distinct for owner review.

proposals.title: Ephesians: from grace received to a life of love
proposals.question: How does the whole letter hold together, and which sources help me read each part?
proposals.opening: Ephesians moves from the blessings of belonging to Christ to the life those blessings make possible together. Praise becomes prayer; strangers become one household; the church grows into Christ; love takes shape in ordinary relationships; and the letter ends with strength, prayer and peace. This guide follows all six chapters in that order.
proposals.placement: A complete book guide, with the unity proposal nested in chapter 4.

outline.title: Begin with the letter’s movement
outline.text: Read chapters 1–3 as the announcement of God’s work in Christ and chapters 4–6 as the call to live in keeping with it. The division is a reading aid: prayer, praise and ethical concern run across both halves.

outline.title: Read each chapter in context
outline.text: Each chapter below has a plain-language introduction, an outline covering every verse, two explained commentary readings and a question for reflection.

outline.title: Compare identifiable voices
outline.text: Calvin’s commentary is read in William Pringle’s translation. Fergusson supplies a distinct exposition. Their Reformed interpretations are named; agreement between them is not treated as the whole Christian conversation.

outline.title: Use the related proposals deliberately
outline.text: Unity is a chapter-4 extension. Faith and justification can deepen a question raised in chapter 2; temptation and perseverance can extend chapter 6. Other proposals remain separate rather than being forced into this book.

sourceNotes: Fergusson: a verse-by-verse exposition with practical observations. Read the specified section and its surrounding argument.
Calvin, translated by William Pringle: a commentary with embedded editorial material. The guide distinguishes the commentator from notes.
proposals.limit: The narrative and outline are a new editorial draft. The source readings are traceable; theological agreement and public release have not been approved.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: The parent guide. Its six chapters provide the reading sequence; the other proposals have specific, limited roles below.

proposals.title: Unity is a gift—and a calling
proposals.question: If the church is already one, why does it still need to grow into unity?
proposals.opening: Ephesians 4 asks believers to keep the unity of the Spirit and also describes a unity toward which the body grows. Those statements belong together. The practical question is how humility, patient love and the gifts of ministry serve a community whose life is grounded in Christ.
proposals.placement: Inside the Ephesians guide, chapter 4, after the outline of 4:1–16. This is a deeper section, not a second competing book guide.

outline.title: Keep what has been given: 4:1–6
outline.text: Begin with the command to walk worthily: humility, gentleness, patience and bearing with one another. The repeated “one” language grounds the appeal in a shared Lord, faith, baptism and Father.

outline.title: Grow through gifts: 4:7–16
outline.text: The gifts serve the building up of the body. Maturity is described through knowledge of Christ, stability against deception, truthful love and the contribution of each part.

outline.title: Read Bavinck on unity already present
outline.text: The retained Magnalia Dei passage grounds unity in the Father, Son and Spirit, then says that this unity is still being realized imperfectly in earthly congregations. Read it for the distinction between a given bond and its incomplete expression.

outline.title: Read Waldron on the purpose of ministry
outline.text: Waldron’s selected discussion of 4:13–14 emphasizes the church’s immature understanding and its vulnerability to deception. His wider essay is polemical; this paragraph does not establish the whole of that argument.

outline.title: Bring the comparison back to the chapter
outline.text: Ask how the two emphases illuminate the movement from keeping unity in verse 3 to growing together in verses 13–16. Then read 4:25–32 to see unity expressed in speech, work, anger and forgiveness.

sourceNotes: Waldron: the selected source text is available here; the full held work currently has catalogue access only.
Bavinck: the exact selected discussion is readable on page 27. The modern English witness and its credits need to remain visible.
proposals.limit: These writers support different parts of the reading question. Do not turn the comparison into a claim that they agree on every question of ministry or church order.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: Inside Ephesians 4, especially 4:1–16. This is a deepening section, not another book guide.

proposals.title: Reading the Lord’s Supper with Hodge and Henry
proposals.question: What do the biblical names of the Lord’s Supper help us notice about the meal?
proposals.opening: The names “Lord’s Supper,” “cup of blessing,” “Lord’s table” and “communion” direct attention to different aspects of the same observance. A. A. Hodge gathers those names into a sequence of questions. Matthew Henry supplies a pastoral treatment of why the supper belongs to the Lord. Reading them beside the biblical passages makes their explanations inspectable.
proposals.placement: A guide alongside the institution accounts and 1 Corinthians 10–11.

outline.title: Read the biblical passages first
outline.text: Place Matthew 26:26–28, Mark 14:22–24, Luke 22:17–20 and 1 Corinthians 11:23–30 beside 1 Corinthians 10:16–21. Distinguish the institution narratives from Paul’s discussion of participation and conduct.

outline.title: Use Hodge’s questions as the outline
outline.text: Chapter 43 begins with the institution passages, continued observance and the names of the meal. Read the complete third answer: the saved short extract stopped before it finished explaining communion.

outline.title: Ask why Henry calls it the Lord’s Supper
outline.text: Henry’s section offers a second route into the name and its devotional significance. His held text is a 2017 Chapel Library compilation that declares modernization and omissions; it is not an untouched early edition.

outline.title: Keep exposition and quoted standards distinct
outline.text: Later in Hodge’s chapter, a separately labelled block quotes church standards. Those quotations are evidence of how the standards are represented there, not additional independent authors speaking in Hodge’s own voice.

sourceNotes: A. A. Hodge, Outlines of Theology, chapter 43: read pages 32–33.
Matthew Henry: complete section 2 on page 1; glossary explanations appear separately on page 3.
proposals.limit: The guide presents identified Protestant readings. Any Catholic comparison needs its own primary sources and fair account; Hodge’s polemical account alone cannot represent Catholic teaching.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: Separate passage guide to the Lord’s Supper. It belongs alongside the Ephesians guide in the library, not inside its chapter outline.

proposals.title: How do I go on after loss?
proposals.question: Can hope give direction to life without asking me to pretend that loss is small?
proposals.opening: These readings approach grief from two directions. Miller puts the bereaved person’s question into words: how can a life continue after its hopes have been broken? Spurgeon turns to the hope laid up in heaven and asks what it can sustain in the present. The page should give room for both grief and hope, without treating a historical devotional as a timetable for recovery.
proposals.placement: A short pastoral reading path with two readings in sequence.

outline.title: Begin with the question, not a prescription
outline.text: Miller describes a young bereaved woman facing a future she had not expected. His immediate value is the concrete question of how to go on. His account of providence is his theological interpretation of her situation.

outline.title: Read Miller’s longer answer
outline.text: Follow the surrounding discussion in The Book of Comfort before extracting an instruction from it. Do not repeat his statements about God’s plan as though the page knows why a particular person suffered a loss.

outline.title: Read Spurgeon’s October 2 morning meditation
outline.text: Spurgeon connects Colossians 1:5 with rest, holiness and the ending of bereavement. His emphasis is the sustaining force of future hope amid present weariness.

outline.title: End with a small reflection
outline.text: Which part of the reading gives language to your grief, and which offers hope? The page can invite a reader to sit with those two questions rather than demand an immediate emotional change.

sourceNotes: Miller: a retained passage is available below; the full copy is currently catalogue-only in the reader.
Spurgeon: October 2 morning reading, exact passage on page 23.
proposals.limit: Present this as optional historical pastoral reading, not a diagnosis, explanation of an individual loss or promise of rapid relief.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: A separate pastoral path. It can follow reflection on comfort and prayer in Ephesians 6, but its selected authors are not commenting on that chapter.

proposals.title: When prayer feels dry
proposals.question: How have earlier Christians described prayer when consolation seems absent?
proposals.opening: Rous and Whitefield give different vocabularies for an experience that can be difficult to name. Rous speaks of thirsty and weary souls receiving consolation as a gift. Whitefield places dryness in prayer within a sermon that also addresses spiritual pride and temptation. The order and setting matter: isolated sentences can sound like a diagnosis of a reader that the sources do not justify.
proposals.placement: A focused reading path about prayer, with historical language explained.

outline.title: Name the experience carefully
outline.text: Distinguish a lack of felt consolation from a settled judgment about someone’s faith. The page’s question is how these writers understand the experience, not whether their categories explain every reader.

outline.title: Read Rous on consolation as gift
outline.text: His imagery moves through thirst, weariness, mourning, water and wine. Read it as theological and devotional imagery rather than a formula for producing a feeling.

outline.title: Follow Whitefield’s transition
outline.text: The saved window first addresses spiritual pride and only then introduces deadness and dryness in prayer. Read across pages 10–11 to retain that transition.

outline.title: Compare the emphasis
outline.text: Rous emphasizes the source of consolation; Whitefield’s sermon provides a pastoral framework for responding to difficulty. Ask what each contributes and what remains unaddressed.

sourceNotes: Rous: selected text is supplied, with full-reader access still pending.
Whitefield: the selected source crosses pages 10–11; transcription gaps remain visible.
proposals.limit: Do not infer from either passage that every experience of dryness is caused by pride or proves spiritual failure.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: An optional pastoral extension of the prayers in Ephesians 1 and 3. Its source passages must keep their own setting.

proposals.title: Forgiveness after injury
proposals.question: What reasons do these writers give for forgiving someone who has wronged us?
proposals.opening: Tillotson reasons from our own need for mercy and from Christ’s example. Winslow dwells on the pain of injury, including injury from fellow Christians, and turns toward forgiving love. A useful page lets the reader follow both arguments rather than reduce them to a command to stop feeling hurt.
proposals.placement: A pastoral comparison; an optional extension from Ephesians 4:31–5:2.

outline.title: State the injury honestly
outline.text: Winslow explicitly acknowledges being misunderstood and wounded, including by friends and fellow believers. Keep that recognition before his exhortation.

outline.title: Follow Tillotson’s reasoning
outline.text: He argues that those who need forgiveness should be ready to forgive, then contrasts human retaliation with divine mercy and Christ’s example.

outline.title: Read Winslow’s devotional appeal
outline.text: His attention rests on Christ’s forgiving love and on learning to pray for enemies. Compare this with Tillotson’s more discursive argument.

outline.title: Keep the question precise
outline.text: The comparison concerns the reasons for forgiveness. It does not, by itself, settle questions of restored trust, reconciliation, accountability or continued exposure to harm.

sourceNotes: Tillotson: a sermon with a located held-text passage.
Winslow: the retained devotional passage is available; its full reader copy is not yet offered.
proposals.limit: The two selections do not provide a complete treatment of reconciliation or the handling of continuing abuse.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: A practical extension of Ephesians 4:31–5:2. The selected authors provide a comparison, not additional direct commentary on every verse.

proposals.title: What sustains faith under pressure?
proposals.question: How do Brooks and Goodwin describe the resources of a Christian facing temptation?
proposals.opening: Brooks presents God as a believer’s portion: a good that makes lesser inducements lose their claim. Goodwin emphasizes the power of God both beginning and sustaining faith. The comparison is useful because one passage attends to what the heart values, while the other attends to what keeps faith alive.
proposals.placement: A comparative reading, with a thematic link from Ephesians 6:10–18.

outline.title: Read Brooks’s argument about treasure
outline.text: His selected passage argues that enjoying God as one’s portion strengthens resistance to temptation. Historical examples in the passage are illustrations supplied by Brooks, not newly verified biographies.

outline.title: Read Goodwin on sustaining power
outline.text: Goodwin describes faith being continued, strengthened and preserved, especially under temptation. He directs attention to dependence rather than self-sufficiency.

outline.title: Compare desire and dependence
outline.text: Ask how a changed valuation of good relates to reliance on God’s power. These are complementary questions in the selected passages, not proof that the authors agree in every detail.

outline.title: Return to the reader’s question
outline.text: The page should help a reader identify the argument being made and the Scripture each writer uses. It should not imply that the metaphor “temptation-proof” guarantees a person cannot fall.

sourceNotes: Brooks: full reader access is pending; the exact selected text remains available here.
Goodwin: selected discussion on page 36.
proposals.limit: The passages are thematic companions to Ephesians 6, not both direct expositions of that chapter.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: A thematic extension after Ephesians 6:10–20. The comparison concerns spiritual pressure and endurance; do not relabel its source passages as Ephesians exposition.

proposals.title: What does faith do in justification?
proposals.question: Is faith described as the ground of justification, or as the means of receiving it?
proposals.opening: Boyce’s short catechism distinguishes the instrument of justification from its cause. Gill’s discussion is longer and includes positions he reports in order to reject. A clear comparison first defines the question, then follows each author’s distinctions before identifying the limited point they can be compared on.
proposals.placement: A doctrinal comparison, available as an optional extension from Ephesians 2:8–10.

outline.title: Define the terms before comparing
outline.text: “Ground” asks on what basis a person is accepted; “instrument” asks how that benefit is received. The page must let the sources specify their terms rather than assume every writer uses them identically.

outline.title: Read Boyce’s complete catechism unit
outline.text: The selected eight-question unit belongs to A Brief Catechism of Bible Doctrine, contained in the held volume labelled Abstract of Systematic Theology. That contained-work distinction belongs in the credit line.

outline.title: Read Gill’s complete faith subsection
outline.text: Use subsection 5a5, including its subdivisions, rather than the earlier fragment. Gill discusses faith or believing while distinguishing Christ, faith’s object, from the act of believing.

outline.title: Keep reported views separate from Gill’s conclusion
outline.text: When Gill introduces what “some” say, that wording identifies a position under discussion. The comparison must show when he is reporting and when he is rejecting a claim.

sourceNotes: Boyce: the complete catechism unit on page 25.
Gill: complete subsection 5a5 on page 58; its proposed inspection interval differs from the old saved fragment.
proposals.limit: This is an identified Baptist/Reformed comparison, not a verdict on all Christian accounts of justification.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: A doctrinal extension after Ephesians 2:8–10. It distinguishes later doctrinal explanation from what the chapter itself says.

proposals.title: Continuing in faith: duty and dependence
proposals.question: How can perseverance be necessary while also depending on God’s preserving power?
proposals.opening: Flavel begins by defining perseverance as continuing in duty and obedience amid opposition. Bunyan insists that reaching the end is necessary, then locates the power to do so in God. Reading definition and ground together makes the comparison more useful than a shared “perseverance” topic label.
proposals.placement: A doctrinal and pastoral comparison; linked to temptation and the Hebrews warning study.

outline.title: Start with Flavel’s definition
outline.text: His question-and-answer form distinguishes continuing in faith from merely having professed it. Read the questions together, including the discussion of people who fall away.

outline.title: Read Bunyan’s journey image
outline.text: Bunyan compares a proposed voyage with actually arriving: a journey interrupted by drowning does not reach its destination. He uses the image to explain why perseverance belongs to his account of complete salvation.

outline.title: Trace the claimed source of strength
outline.text: Bunyan then says that this perseverance depends on the one who began the good work. Flavel likewise moves from definition to the grounds of preservation.

outline.title: Keep warnings in view
outline.text: The page should place claims about preservation alongside the authors’ concern for continuing faith and obedience. It should not turn their teaching into a claim that conduct is irrelevant.

sourceNotes: Flavel: the question sequence begins on page 4.
Bunyan: the selected argument is on page 1.
proposals.limit: These selections share a confessional setting. A broader comparison requires additional, fairly represented readings.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: A thematic extension of Ephesians 6:18 and its call to persevere in prayer. Its broader doctrinal question needs its own page.

proposals.title: Hebrews 8: whose covenant is this?
proposals.question: How do Pink and Gunn connect Jeremiah’s promise with the argument of Hebrews?
proposals.opening: Both selections address the new covenant, but they do different work. Pink uses the promise of law written on the heart against the claim that law has no place in Christian life. Gunn challenges a particular account that separates a church covenant from a future Jewish covenant. The page needs to identify those questions before comparing their answers.
proposals.placement: A Hebrews 8 guide, alongside Hebrews 10:14–18 and Jeremiah 31:31–34.

outline.title: Read the promise in both settings
outline.text: Place Jeremiah’s promise beside its use in Hebrews. Identify the promises quoted and the argument in which Hebrews places them.

outline.title: Read Pink’s question about law
outline.text: Pink argues that writing the law within the people of the covenant is not the same as abolishing it. Present this as his interpretation, with the relevant passage open.

outline.title: Read Gunn’s reported position and reply
outline.text: Gunn describes a two-covenant theory before criticizing it. The words he assigns to that position must not be mistaken for his own conclusion.

outline.title: Name the overlap and the difference
outline.text: Both selections connect the promise to Christians; they address different disputed claims. Two writers arguing against a view do not constitute a balanced account of that view.

sourceNotes: Pink: Law and the Saint, selected Hebrews 8 discussion.
Gunn: the chapter addressing Hebrews and Jeremiah; full reader access is pending for both exact copies.
proposals.limit: A publishable comparison needs the disputed position represented from its own sources, not only from its critics.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: A separate Hebrews 8 comparison. A link from Ephesians 2 may help explore belonging and covenant, but the two passages must retain their distinct arguments.

proposals.title: Hebrews 6: read the warning in its argument
proposals.question: What does the warning say, and which source actually explains that warning?
proposals.opening: The current pairing needs correction in presentation. Pink’s retained passage directly introduces Hebrews 6:4–6. Owen’s retained window concerns instruction, ordinances and inward grace; it is surrounding context, not yet a matched exposition of the same verses. The page should show that difference clearly.
proposals.placement: A Hebrews 5:11–6:20 reading guide, with the direct comparison still incomplete.

outline.title: Read before and after the warning
outline.text: Begin at 5:11, continue through the call to maturity and the warning, and finish with the encouragement and promise later in chapter 6. A single frightening phrase should not replace the argument.

outline.title: Follow Pink’s structure
outline.text: Pink distinguishes progress and perseverance, then considers the persons, the sin and the consequence in the warning. His quotation of Adolph Saphir is another voice and must be credited separately.

outline.title: Use Owen for the question he actually addresses
outline.text: The saved Owen passage contrasts outward observance with inward grace and emphasizes diligent teaching. It can supply context for the discussion but cannot yet stand as his full interpretation of 6:4–6.

outline.title: Show the remaining comparison honestly
outline.text: The useful next addition is Owen’s exact treatment of the warning with its context. Until then, the page offers Pink’s located discussion and a clearly labelled Owen contextual reading.

sourceNotes: Pink: a direct retained discussion of the warning; catalogue access only.
Owen: page 4 contains the contextual passage, not an established parallel answer to 6:4–6.
proposals.limit: The interpretation of this warning is contested. This draft does not use an unmatched pair to manufacture agreement or settle the debate.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: A separate Hebrews 6 guide. It may accompany perseverance as a related question, without being inserted into Ephesians as if Paul were treating the same passage.

proposals.title: Psalm 51 begins with a story
proposals.question: Why should the title of the psalm matter to our reading of repentance?
proposals.opening: Hildersham begins his lectures with the title: David, Nathan’s confrontation and the circumstances of the psalm. That is a useful starting point because repentance is not presented as a detached feeling. The confession belongs to a history of wrongdoing being named and addressed.
proposals.placement: A Psalm 51 introduction focused on its title and setting.

outline.title: Read the title aloud
outline.text: Identify the person, the confrontation and the musical direction named in the title before moving into the body of the psalm.

outline.title: Follow Hildersham’s first lecture
outline.text: He argues that the titles of psalms can illuminate their meaning and should not be discarded as irrelevant. The selected passage directly supports that method of reading.

outline.title: Distinguish the supported claim from a larger proposal
outline.text: The retained opening establishes the importance of the title. A fuller account of public repentance needs the later lecture passages that make that argument, not merely this opening.

outline.title: Read the confession with its setting in view
outline.text: The proposed page would then trace confession, cleansing, renewal and restored praise through Psalm 51, with each section anchored in the biblical text.

sourceNotes: Hildersham: Lecture 1 on the title of Psalm 51; exact text available below, full reader access pending.
proposals.limit: The original candidate’s public-repentance claim is broader than this selected opening. The draft narrows the claim to what can presently be shown.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: A separate Psalm 51 introduction. The selected opening explains how a psalm’s title supplies context; it is not a ready-made section of the Ephesians guide.

proposals.title: What happened to Whitefield’s words in quotation?
proposals.question: Can I follow a modern quotation back to the earlier sermon and see what surrounds it?
proposals.opening: Piper introduces Whitefield’s argument about election and humility. The held Whitefield sermon contains the corresponding wording in a longer argument, including a reference to Mr. Trail. Following that trail helps a reader distinguish the later author’s use of a quotation from the earlier preacher’s own context.
proposals.placement: A source-trail page; an optional historical reading beside Ephesians 1, not a commentary on that chapter.

outline.title: Identify the later quotation
outline.text: Piper explicitly names Whitefield. The surrounding modern chapter also discusses other writers; the heading and transition show where the Whitefield quotation begins.

outline.title: Open the earlier sermon
outline.text: Read Whitefield’s claim in the held sermon before and after the quoted portion. His argument concerns election, humility and boasting in the Lord.

outline.title: Keep the damaged place visible
outline.text: The earlier transcription contains an illegible gap where the later quotation supplies readable wording. The later quotation is not permission to silently repair the held witness.

outline.title: Separate three voices
outline.text: Label Piper’s framing, Whitefield’s sermon and the appeal Whitefield attributes to Trail. The trail does not independently verify Trail’s original wording or the complete transmission between editions.

sourceNotes: Piper: the named quotation and framing are on page 2.
Whitefield: the located sermon witness retains historical spelling and an encoded gap.
proposals.limit: A matching passage establishes a useful quotation trail; it does not prove that the exact held edition was Piper’s direct source.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: A source-reading aid for tracing Whitefield through later quotation. It supports the trustworthiness of the library rather than explaining a chapter of Ephesians.

proposals.title: Discernment without invented motives
proposals.question: What is the difference between evaluating an action and claiming to know a person’s hidden motives?
proposals.opening: Godolphin lists ways people injure a neighbour’s reputation: false rumours, suspicion and taking words in the worst sense. Pink makes a related distinction between matters actually before us and presumptuous judgments built on unconfirmed claims. The comparison can sharpen a concrete ethical question without making “judge not” mean that evidence never matters.
proposals.placement: An ethical reading; a companion to forgiveness, rather than a duplicate of it.

outline.title: Start with reputation and evidence
outline.text: Godolphin’s list places unjust judgment among practices that damage a neighbour. Keep its list format and moral setting visible.

outline.title: Read Pink’s distinction
outline.text: Pink explicitly distinguishes authenticated facts from mere suspicions and unconfirmed rumours. That distinction is more specific than a general prohibition of all judgment.

outline.title: Compare the scope of responsibility
outline.text: Ask what each source treats as legitimately within a person’s responsibility, and what it calls an intrusion into matters the person cannot know.

outline.title: Apply the question, not a verdict
outline.text: A reflection can ask: What do I know? What have I inferred? What motive have I supplied without evidence? The page should not judge a named contemporary dispute on the reader’s behalf.

sourceNotes: Godolphin: a located list within a larger compilation; source independence is not inferred.
Pink: a retained 1941 Studies in the Scriptures passage; full reader access pending.
proposals.limit: Shared biblical references establish relevance for comparison, not literary borrowing or independent corroboration.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: A possible ethical extension of Ephesians 4:15 and 6:12. Its main subject is discerning claims without pretending to know another person’s motives.

proposals.title: The word received, resisted and misunderstood
proposals.question: What does each author mean when he says God’s word accomplishes its purpose?
proposals.opening: Haldane places Isaiah 55 and 2 Corinthians 2 within an argument about redemption. Sikes uses a related reference pattern while warning against treating divine teaching as material for intellectual display. The shared texts invite inspection, but their larger arguments are sufficiently different that this should remain an exploratory comparison.
proposals.placement: A secondary study of Scripture and preaching, after stronger guides are established.

outline.title: Read the two biblical images
outline.text: Isaiah 55 speaks of the word accomplishing its purpose; 2 Corinthians 2 uses the contrasting imagery of life and death. Read their own contexts first.

outline.title: Locate Haldane’s use
outline.text: His selected passage moves from those texts into Christ’s love for the church in Ephesians 5:25–27. The transition belongs to his argument in The Doctrine of the Atonement.

outline.title: Locate Sikes’s concern
outline.text: Sikes criticizes curiosity and notional discourse that serves self-exaltation. His surrounding spiritual categories require explanation before the passage can be recommended as a straightforward devotional.

outline.title: Make the comparison modest
outline.text: The page can show two uses of related biblical texts. It cannot infer a common complete doctrine, influence or consensus from that overlap.

sourceNotes: Haldane: the selected text is available, while the exact full reader copy remains pending.
Sikes: a located historical exposition requiring particular attention to the surrounding argument.
proposals.limit: Haldane cites Ephesians 5, but the saved proposal’s purpose is word-effects. It should not be passed off as another main chapter-5 commentary.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: A separate exploratory comparison. One source quotes Ephesians 5:25–27 within another argument; that quotation is a limited link, not a second chapter-5 commentary.

proposals.title: Knowing God: relationship, trust and response
proposals.question: What do Purnell and Warner ask of a reader when they speak about knowing God?
proposals.opening: Purnell contrasts true, though imperfect, knowledge of God with ignorance. Warner uses John 17 and 2 Thessalonians 1 within a sermon about peace in troubled times. The same references serve different immediate purposes: one passage is a topical explanation, the other an appeal within a public sermon.
proposals.placement: A secondary historical reading on knowing God, with an optional thematic connection to Ephesians’ prayers.

outline.title: Read Purnell’s distinction
outline.text: His section says that regenerate people truly know God while their knowledge remains imperfect. That distinction can help frame a question about growth without assuming complete understanding.

outline.title: Read Warner in his sermon setting
outline.text: Warner moves from providence and public trouble to the call to make peace with God. Preserve that setting rather than present his words as an abstract definition.

outline.title: Compare the use of John 17:3
outline.text: Both use the language of eternal life and knowing God. Ask what role the verse plays in each argument, rather than counting the common reference as an answer.

outline.title: Return to the wider reading
outline.text: The relation to Ephesians 1 and 3 is thematic: growth in knowledge and prayer. Neither selected passage is being offered as direct exposition of those chapters.

sourceNotes: Purnell: the section headed Of the knowledge of God.
Warner: the selected application in the 1688 sermon.
proposals.limit: The saved selections do not establish dependence between the authors or justify a synthesis of their whole theologies.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: A thematic extension of Ephesians 1:17–19 and 3:14–19. Its historical comparison can deepen the question of knowing, but its source passages are not direct exposition of those prayers.

proposals.title: Why these churches published a confession
proposals.question: What does the 1644 document say it is trying to explain or defend?
proposals.opening: The preface presents the confession as a public statement by churches responding to accusations against them. A useful introduction starts with that stated purpose, distinguishes it from an independent history of the controversy, and lets the reader inspect the document’s own wording.
proposals.placement: A historical document introduction attached to the confession, not another general church-history essay.

outline.title: Identify the document
outline.text: Display the 1644 imprint and the collective church attribution with the source’s own title. A title-page date is not a complete publication history.

outline.title: Explain its stated purpose
outline.text: The opening says the churches are setting out their faith for examination and answering charges made in pulpit and print. That is their account of the intervention they are making.

outline.title: Keep the collective voice intact
outline.text: Do not turn the preface into a statement by a single named theologian. The subscription and signatories need edition-specific verification.

outline.title: Lead into the confession itself
outline.text: The page should orient the reader to the document’s form and then offer the text. Any account of its opponents or reception belongs in a separately sourced historical section.

sourceNotes: The held preface and subscription support the collective attribution; independent print and signatory checks remain incomplete.
proposals.limit: The document’s account of accusations is evidence of its self-presentation, not independent proof that every accusation was false.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: A separate document introduction. It gives context for one Baptist confession and can support doctrinal comparisons; it is not part of the Ephesians chapter sequence.

proposals.title: A theology textbook in its educational setting
proposals.question: What can the book’s own title and dedication tell us about why it was written?
proposals.opening: The held title names Boyce’s professorship, and the dedication connects theological education with an endowed chair and the preparation of ministers. Those are useful facts for introducing this work. They should enrich the existing work page rather than become an inflated biography based on two pieces of front matter.
proposals.placement: A short introduction on Boyce’s work page; supporting context for the justification comparison.

outline.title: Read the title as a source
outline.text: Identify the named author, professorship and institution exactly as the held title presents them. Keep the edition’s displayed publication statement distinct from independently checked bibliography.

outline.title: Read the dedication as a statement of purpose
outline.text: The dedication praises support for theological education and the Christian ministry. It helps explain the book’s institutional setting and intended use.

outline.title: Connect the work to the reader’s task
outline.text: A reader opening a systematic theology should know that the volume belongs to a setting of organized theological instruction. That context is useful without claiming to explain all of Boyce’s intellectual development.

outline.title: Keep the two held witnesses distinct
outline.text: The profile source is an XML witness. The justification passage comes from a catechism contained in a different held EPUB. Shared author and container labels do not erase that distinction.

sourceNotes: Boyce title/dedication: the XML witness credited to CCEL; full reader access for this exact copy remains pending.
proposals.limit: Front matter supports a narrow work introduction, not a full independent biography or a merged edition identity.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: A separate work introduction. It helps identify the Boyce material used in the justification comparison and prevents a textbook and an embedded catechism from being treated as the same unit.

proposals.title: “Charity,” caritas and “love” on one page
proposals.question: What can an actual bilingual page show—and what can it not settle?
proposals.opening: The selected Corinthians witness places English “Charity” beside Latin caritas in a Scripture table. The adjoining translated commentary begins with “Love is patient.” Seeing the table and commentary together gives a concrete example of vocabulary in an edition without pretending that one alignment settles every translation choice.
proposals.placement: A small reading note beside 1 Corinthians 13:4–8.

outline.title: Identify the two kinds of text
outline.text: The English/Latin columns are Scripture text. The following English explanation is translated commentary. They are not one uninterrupted paragraph by Calvin.

outline.title: Read the local correspondence
outline.text: Compare the parallel wording at the same verse number. Preserve the original joined form Caritaspatiens as a transcription observation rather than inventing a new dictionary headword.

outline.title: Credit the translation correctly
outline.text: The native header and title identify Rev. John Pringle for this Corinthians volume. Ephesians separately credits William Pringle.

outline.title: Inspect the notes as notes
outline.text: The adjacent commentary includes editorial notes, some signed Ed. and one unsigned. Their role and individual authorship are different questions.

sourceNotes: Calvin Corinthians, volume 1, translated by John Pringle: Scripture table on page 21; adjoining commentary across pages 21–22.
proposals.limit: The exact Scripture translation provenance is not newly established, and this one correspondence is not a general translation rule.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: A separate language note, with an optional link from Ephesians 5’s theme of love. Its actual table comes from a different biblical passage and cannot settle Ephesians vocabulary.

proposals.title: Who is speaking in this commentary?
proposals.question: How can I tell the author’s explanation from translation, quotation and editorial intervention?
proposals.opening: A commentary page can contain several voices. In the Genesis witness, a note marked Ed. discusses a possible Latin reading, vocatio or vacatio. The note’s conjecture is part of the edition’s apparatus; it should not become Calvin’s unqualified claim or silently alter the source text.
proposals.placement: A reusable source-role explanation in the reader, demonstrated with Genesis and applied to Ephesians.

outline.title: Begin with the complete note
outline.text: Show the complete conjectural note, its Ed. signature and its relation to the passage. Keep the return-link symbol outside a proposed quotation.

outline.title: Explain the edition-level evidence
outline.text: The title and translator’s preface support John King’s translator/editor role in this edition. The selected note itself is signed only Ed.; that distinction should remain visible.

outline.title: Apply the distinction in Ephesians
outline.text: Three Ephesians locating samples enter notes: an unsigned bilingual gloss, a Chandler-labelled quotation and a Bloomfield-labelled quotation. Those voices must be separated before a short extract is presented as Calvin’s explanation.

outline.title: Give readers a usable habit
outline.text: Read the credit, look for note boundaries, and distinguish a source’s assertion from an editor’s hypothesis. The purpose is better understanding, not merely a warning icon.

sourceNotes: Genesis complete note: page 5; title and preface evidence on page 1.
Ephesians note examples: pages 11 and 16 of the William Pringle witness.
proposals.limit: An Ed. signature identifies a role. Personal attribution requires additional edition evidence; it does not transfer automatically across works or modern wrappers.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: A reader aid used throughout the guide, especially with Calvin’s editions. The Genesis example teaches separation of author, translator and editorial note; it is not Ephesians exposition.

proposals.title: Two entries, two languages: “father”
proposals.question: Which entry am I looking at, and how does a gloss help without deciding a verse’s meaning for me?
proposals.opening: The held lexicon has distinct Hebrew אָב and Aramaic אַב entries. The Hebrew entry gives a range of literal and figurative applications; the Aramaic record supplies “father” in a usage field. Keeping the entries and fields distinct is more useful than offering one undifferentiated translation button.
proposals.placement: A compact dictionary aid; separate from the Greek text of Ephesians.

outline.title: Show the term and language together
outline.text: Display Hebrew אָב and Aramaic אַב with their own language labels and preserved diacritics. Similar forms do not make the entries interchangeable.

outline.title: Name the field being quoted
outline.text: The Hebrew wording is a meaning aid; the Aramaic target here is usage. The interface should say which kind of lexicon field the reader is consulting.

outline.title: Keep the entry identity and credit
outline.text: A small entry can still carry a precise source and editorial credit. Do not invent a translator or discard the short script because it is brief.

outline.title: Return to the verse for meaning
outline.text: A dictionary can supply possible senses. Context still determines how a word is being used, and a gloss alone does not decide the interpretation of a passage.

sourceNotes: Hebrew entry H1: original term, preserved with its diacritics.
Hebrew entry H1: the meaning field supplies this English aid.
Aramaic entry H2: original term, distinct from the Hebrew entry.
Aramaic entry H2: the usage field supplies “father.”; it is not labelled as the meaning field.
proposals.limit: This is not an Ephesians vocabulary panel: Ephesians is Greek. The aid remains a separate proposal and protected short-script control.
proposals.relationshipToEphesians: A protected short-entry control and standalone dictionary aid. Hebrew and Aramaic “father” entries must not be used to establish the Greek meaning of “Father” in Ephesians.

chapters.title: Blessing that becomes prayer
chapters.question: What have we received in Christ—and what do we still need to understand?
chapters.introduction: The letter begins with gifts before it gives commands. Paul blesses God for redemption, adoption and an inheritance in Christ, then prays that his readers will know the hope and power already at work among them. Belonging and growing in understanding belong together.

sections.title: A greeting of grace and peace
sections.text: The greeting identifies Paul as an apostle and addresses the saints and faithful in Christ Jesus. Grace and peace introduce the life the rest of the letter unfolds.

sections.title: Chosen and adopted, to the praise of grace
sections.text: The blessing reaches back before the foundation of the world and names adoption through Jesus Christ. Read its language of choosing within this movement of thanksgiving, holiness and love.

sections.title: Redemption, an inheritance and the promised Spirit
sections.text: Forgiveness comes through Christ; God’s purpose gathers all things in him. The Spirit seals the believing recipients and is the earnest of their inheritance. Notice the repeated movement toward the praise of God’s glory.

sections.title: A prayer for opened eyes
sections.text: Paul gives thanks for faith and love, then prays for knowledge of God, hope and power. The resurrection and exaltation of Christ give the prayer its scale; the church is named as his body.

readings.title: Calvin on praise and election
readings.why: Calvin reads the blessing as an invitation to gratitude grounded in God’s grace. His explanation of election is a specifically Reformed interpretation of the passage.
readings.lookFor: Follow the movement from praise to its cause. Compare the claims Calvin makes with the words and purpose of verses 3–6.

readings.title: Fergusson on receiving blessings gratefully
readings.why: Fergusson treats the opening as active thanksgiving, not a detached list of doctrines. He connects the spiritual blessings to God’s work through Christ.
readings.lookFor: Ask how a truth about belonging becomes thanksgiving. Do not treat the two Reformed commentators as independent proof of every disputed conclusion.

chapters.reflection: Which part of Paul’s prayer would help you move from knowing religious words to understanding the hope they describe?
chapters.transition: Chapter 2 shows this power at work in people made alive and in a divided people brought together.
chapters.carefulReading: The letter’s language about election has a long history of disagreement. This guide names the selected commentators’ readings without presenting them as the only Christian reading.

chapters.title: Made alive, brought near
chapters.question: How does grace create both a new life and a new people?
chapters.introduction: The chapter moves from death to life and from distance to belonging. Its two movements belong together: salvation by grace leads to good works, and reconciliation to God makes former strangers fellow citizens and members of one household.

sections.title: The former life
sections.text: Paul recalls a life shaped by trespasses, disobedience and destructive desires. The recollection includes both “you” and “we”; it prepares for mercy rather than supplying a reason for superiority.

sections.title: Mercy, faith and a life of good works
sections.text: God makes people alive with Christ because of his mercy and love. Salvation is described as gift, excluding boasting; the same passage calls the recipients God’s workmanship, created for good works.

sections.title: Those far away are brought near
sections.text: Gentile exclusion is recalled so that the change through Christ can be understood. Christ makes peace, reconciles both groups to God through the cross, and gives both access to the Father through one Spirit.

sections.title: A household and a growing temple
sections.text: The strangers become fellow citizens and members of God’s household. The image changes to a building joined together in Christ and growing into a dwelling for God.

readings.title: Calvin on grace received through faith
readings.why: Calvin explains salvation as freely given and faith as receiving rather than earning it. This helps distinguish the ground of salvation from the good works described immediately afterward.
readings.lookFor: Read through verse 10. Does your account of grace leave room for the life of good works the passage describes?

readings.title: Fergusson on gift and boasting
readings.why: Fergusson describes faith as the instrument that receives Christ and insists that salvation, from beginning to end, depends on grace. His account belongs to his Reformed theological framework.
readings.lookFor: Notice which kind of boasting verses 8–9 exclude, then bring the argument into conversation with the shared belonging in verses 11–22.

chapters.reflection: Where do you tend to separate personal salvation from the shared life of people brought near to one another?
chapters.transition: Chapter 3 explains why Gentile participation in this one body is central to Paul’s ministry.
chapters.carefulReading: Jew and Gentile name the historical division in Paul’s argument. Do not turn the passage, or older commentary’s polemical language, into a charge against Jewish people. Calvin’s chapter-2 units also contain editorial notes; those notes are separate voices.

chapters.title: A shared inheritance, a love beyond measure
chapters.question: What does it mean to belong together—and to know Christ’s love together?
chapters.introduction: Paul explains his ministry in light of the mystery now made known: Gentiles share the inheritance, the body and the promise in Christ. He then returns to prayer, asking for inward strength and a knowledge of Christ’s love shared with all the saints.

sections.title: The mystery is made known
sections.text: Paul’s explanation interrupts the opening “for this cause.” The mystery is not an unexplained spiritual secret: verse 6 identifies Gentiles as fellow heirs, of the same body, and fellow participants in the promise through the gospel.

sections.title: Ministry, wisdom and suffering
sections.text: Paul describes his ministry as a gift of grace. The church makes known God’s manifold wisdom; his imprisonment and tribulations are not to make the readers lose heart.

sections.title: Strength to know Christ’s love
sections.text: The prayer asks for strengthening through the Spirit, Christ dwelling in their hearts through faith, and roots in love. Its dimensions are explored with all the saints; knowing a love that surpasses knowledge is more than collecting information.

sections.title: Praise beyond the limits of asking
sections.text: The chapter ends in praise to the God whose power exceeds what the readers can ask or imagine, with glory in the church and in Christ Jesus.

readings.title: Calvin on Christ dwelling in the heart
readings.why: Calvin distinguishes an inward reception of Christ from merely speaking about him or carrying ideas in the mind. His reading connects faith, the Spirit’s work and a love that takes root.
readings.lookFor: Keep the plural setting in view: Paul’s prayer is for people learning to grasp this love together.

readings.title: Fergusson on fellow heirs
readings.why: Fergusson links the three shared realities in verse 6: inheritance, membership in one body and participation in the promise. The gospel, rather than circumcision, is central to his explanation of Gentile inclusion.
readings.lookFor: Find the three expressions in verse 6 before following the commentary’s theological deductions.

chapters.reflection: How would your understanding of spiritual growth change if “with all saints” remained central to it?
chapters.transition: The “therefore” of chapter 4 turns this shared calling into a shared manner of life.
chapters.carefulReading: The thematic proposals on knowing God and dry prayer may extend reflection here. They are not additional verse-by-verse witnesses to Paul’s argument.

chapters.title: One body, growing into Christ
chapters.question: How is unity both something to keep and something to grow toward?
chapters.introduction: Paul calls the church to live in a way worthy of its calling. The chapter moves from one body and one Spirit to diverse gifts and growing maturity, then to the everyday practices that make a renewed common life visible.

sections.title: Keep the unity already given
sections.text: Humility, gentleness, patience and forbearance serve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. The repeated “one” statements give this calling its foundation.

sections.title: Receive gifts and grow together
sections.text: Christ gives gifts for ministry and the building up of his body. Unity, knowledge and maturity are goals of this growth; truth spoken in love and every part’s contribution replace instability and manipulation.

sections.title: Put off the old life; put on the new
sections.text: The readers are called away from their former manner of life. Learning Christ involves renewal of the mind and a new life marked by righteousness and holiness.

sections.title: Make renewal tangible
sections.text: Truthful speech, responsible anger, honest work and sharing, words that build up, kindness and forgiveness give the chapter’s teaching concrete form. Membership in one another is part of the reason.

readings.title: Calvin on gifts that build the body
readings.why: Calvin examines the wording of ministry and edification and argues for the church’s need of teaching and pastoral ministry. His reading resists an entirely self-sufficient approach to understanding Scripture.
readings.lookFor: Read verses 11–16 as one movement. Ask who is equipped, what is built, and how love shapes the result.

readings.title: Fergusson on maturity still ahead
readings.why: Fergusson understands full unity and maturity as a goal finally reached at the last day. This gives a useful question for the chapter: how do present gifts serve a completion the church has not yet reached?
readings.lookFor: Distinguish the unity to keep in verse 3 from the unity to attain in verse 13, without treating the church’s present growth as unimportant.

chapters.reflection: Which practice in verses 25–32 would make “building up the body” concrete in your relationships this week?
chapters.transition: Chapter 5 carries this renewed life forward as walking in love, light and wisdom.
chapters.carefulReading: The existing unity proposal belongs inside this chapter. Its Bavinck and Waldron readings deepen verses 1–16; they are not a second competing Ephesians guide. Unity does not erase the need to test teaching or address harm.

chapters.title: Walk in love, light and wisdom
chapters.question: What does Christ’s self-giving love change in ordinary conduct and relationships?
chapters.introduction: The call to imitate God takes its shape from Christ’s love. Paul connects this pattern to speech, desires, wise use of time, worship and the household. The household passage must be read within that sustained concern for love, rather than detached into isolated instructions.

sections.title: Walk in the love Christ has shown
sections.text: The chapter continues the preceding call to forgiveness. Christ’s self-giving is both the pattern of love and an offering to God.

sections.title: Live as children of light
sections.text: Sexual wrongdoing, covetousness and destructive speech are set against thanksgiving and goodness, righteousness and truth. The readers are to discern what pleases the Lord and expose works of darkness.

sections.title: Attend to how you walk
sections.text: Wisdom includes attention to time and understanding the Lord’s will. The contrast between drunkenness and being filled with the Spirit leads to shared song, thanksgiving and worship.

sections.title: Submission, marriage and Christ’s care
sections.text: The call to submit to one another leads into instructions to wives and husbands. Husbands are commanded to love with Christ’s self-giving care for the church; the passage ends with love and respect. Keep verse 21, the creation quotation and the Christ–church comparison in view together.

readings.title: Calvin on love as self-giving
readings.why: Calvin connects Christ’s reconciling sacrifice with the command to love neighbours. Doctrine and conduct are joined: what Christ has done becomes the pattern for the readers’ treatment of others.
readings.lookFor: Ask how verse 2 continues the kindness and forgiveness of 4:32 before moving to the household passage.

readings.title: Fergusson on the purpose of loving actions
readings.why: Fergusson carries the previous chapter’s forgiveness into the command to love. He asks not only whether an action looks loving, but whether it seeks the neighbour’s good and edification.
readings.lookFor: Trace the motive and purpose of an action. How do the later commands about speech and thanksgiving test it?

chapters.reflection: What would it mean for love to shape both the purpose of your actions and the way you exercise responsibility?
chapters.transition: Chapter 6 continues the household instructions before returning to the strength and prayer the whole church needs.
chapters.carefulReading: Christians differ over the application of the household instructions. This guide does not settle that debate or use the passage to justify coercion or abuse. The caritas proposal concerns a different passage and translation table; it cannot establish the Greek wording of this chapter. The saved Calvin 5:21–27 locating excerpt crosses two reader pages.

chapters.title: Live responsibly; stand and pray
chapters.question: How are ordinary duties and spiritual endurance held together?
chapters.introduction: The letter concludes with responsibilities in the household, strength in the Lord, the armour of God and persevering prayer. Its final personal news, peace and blessing keep the teaching connected to a community of real people.

sections.title: Children and parents
sections.text: Children are instructed to obey and honour their parents; fathers are warned against provoking their children and charged with their nurture. Read the responsibilities in both directions.

sections.title: Enslaved people and masters
sections.text: Paul addresses enslaved people within an ancient social relationship and then addresses masters, including a command to stop threatening. Both answer to a Master in heaven who shows no partiality. This is not simply a description of modern employment.

sections.title: Stand in strength supplied by the Lord
sections.text: The readers are told to be strong in the Lord and put on God’s armour. Truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation and the word of God shape resistance; other people are not identified as the ultimate enemy.

sections.title: Pray for all the saints—and for boldness
sections.text: Prayer accompanies the armour. Paul asks for alertness and perseverance in prayer for all the saints, and for boldness to make the gospel known while he is an ambassador in bonds.

sections.title: News, comfort, peace and grace
sections.text: Tychicus will bring news and comfort their hearts. The final blessing joins peace, love, faith and grace to the community’s life.

readings.title: Calvin on armour meant to be used
readings.why: Calvin treats the armour as resources offered by the Lord that require vigilant use. His image is practical: protection does no good if it remains unused.
readings.lookFor: Keep the repeated call to stand beside the command to pray. The passage does not invite treating a neighbour as a spiritual enemy.

readings.title: Fergusson on strength for the duties already named
readings.why: Fergusson links the concluding exhortation to the preceding duties. Knowing what to do is not the same as having strength to do it; dependence on the Lord belongs to practical obedience.
readings.lookFor: Look backward to chapters 4–6 before treating the armour as an isolated topic. What ordinary duty needs this strength?

chapters.reflection: For whom could you pray with the alertness and perseverance described here—and what would faithful responsibility look like alongside that prayer?
chapters.transition: Return to the opening prayer in chapter 1: the power Paul asks the readers to know is the strength on which their shared life depends.
chapters.carefulReading: The passage addresses slavery in its historical setting. Do not soften that reality into a modern workplace analogy, claim the selected commentators abolish it, or make obedience a warrant for exploitation.
